name: Market Fit
description: A coaching skill that helps a person carve one clear, customer-named offer out of a large body of work, and grow their own judgment while doing it.

examples.label: A university lab's open-source library
examples.brief: A lab built a library that matches patient records across hospital datasets. A few labs use it. Target: a research coordinator understands it after one read.
examples.to_says: Says: each patient shows up once.
examples.started: A scalable, graph-based entity resolution toolkit for biomedical data.
examples.got_to: Merge your sites and trust the patient count.

dips.note: Naming drops at Teach: a skeptic's question made the user doubt a name they liked. Standards rose faster than the draft.
Reasoning drops at the first Test: a confident answer met a miss, then recovered higher.

fit: Customer
A research coordinator merging three hospitals' data before a grant report
Expensive problem
The same patient appears under different spellings and IDs, so counts are wrong
Cost today
Weeks of hand-matching per report (user's estimate, unverified)
Riskiest assumption
Coordinators can run it without IT approval
Evidence
Met in a mock read. No signal from real coordinators yet.
decisions: Find: coordinator over data scientist, because "they get blamed when the count is wrong."
Name: OneRecord over CleanCohort, because "cohort is a word only epidemiologists love."
Teach: lead with "nothing to install," because "IT just needs a line."
examples.next: Start on Evidence. Talk to three real coordinators before round three.

examples.label: A hospital staffing startup
examples.outcome: Target met after splitting the customer
examples.brief: Two founders built an app that fills open nursing shifts. Pilots stall after the demo. Target: a nurse manager asks for a trial after one demo.
examples.started: An AI-powered workforce orchestration engine for healthcare.
examples.got_to: One tap and the shift is covered by someone qualified.

dips.note: Customer drops at the first Test: managers and staff nurses wanted different things. The card held two customers.
Naming drops at the second Find: splitting the customer made the old name wrong.

fit: Customer
A nurse manager getting a call-out at 5am
Expensive problem
Filling a last-minute gap means a phone tree and guesswork about who is eligible
Cost today
About an hour per call-out, plus overtime when nobody answers (founders' estimate)
Riskiest assumption
Staff answer a text faster than a phone call
Evidence
Two of three mock managers asked for a trial. No paid pilot yet.
decisions: Find, round two: nurse manager over staff nurse, because "managers pay; nurses just answer texts."
Name: Covered over ShiftSwap, because "it says what the manager gets at 5am."
Show: drop the scheduling dashboard from the demo, because "nobody asked for a dashboard."
examples.next: Start on Evidence. Run one real pilot on one ward.

examples.label: A campus study app that stalled
examples.outcome: Stopped: no costly problem found yet
examples.brief: A teaching team built an AI study companion. Students try it once. Target: a student says why they'd come back, unprompted.
examples.to_says: The skill stopped before naming. That was the right call.
examples.started: A mesh of AI study agents that personalizes learning.
examples.got_to: We don't know which students lose sleep over this. We're going to ask ten of them.

dips.note: Reasoning drops at the first Test: a polished pitch met a shrug, and the user could not say why.

fit: Customer
First-year students in large lecture courses (still a category)
Expensive problem
Unknown. No pain sentence passed the Find gate in two rounds.
Cost today
Unknown. The skill asked twice and did not invent one.
Riskiest assumption
That students feel a problem worth changing habits for
Evidence
Missed twice. Stopped by the stall rule.
decisions: Find, round two: keep "first-years" over "all students," because "they're the ones who drop out."
Test: stop instead of a third round, because "we're guessing, and guessing faster won't help."
examples.next: Start on Problem. Interview ten first-years about their worst week before running again.
